newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Capitalist boons still a mirage in Balkan region.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Capitalist boons still a mirage in Balkan region.

text.p: More than half a decade after communism began to crumble across Eastern Europe, a majority of the region's southeastern countries have yet to experience of economic prosperity and political stability.
With few exceptions, the economies in the region are in tatters, plagued by high political tensions, erratic growth, high inflation, empty state coffers and obsolete infrastructure.

Most of the post-communist governments in the region failed to use the enthusiasm of the early 1990s to embark on a radical economic reform that has since propelled their northern neighbours to relative prosperity.
For most of them painful reforms, that are already history in Poland or Hungary, are only now being started.

"The euphoria of the early 1990s is gone. The conviction is taking hold that mistakes have been made, that maybe they didn't choose the best available path," said Peter Svoboda, Eastern Europe analyst at Investmentbank Austria.
"The economies are in ruins, and on the political level the sparks haven't fanned out yet. The consolidation phase will last well into the next millenium.".

On the face of it, Bulgaria and Romania want as much as Poland or Czech Republic to join the European Union early in the next century. But in reality, even over-optimistic politicians must admit that it is even difficult to set a realistic target date for their entry.
CROATIA AND SLOVENIA PROSPER

Analysts single out the two ex-Yugoslav republics of Croatia and Slovenia as having the region's best prospects, setting them apart from their neighbours further down the Balkan peninsula. Both have done away with their communist legacy, embraced wide-ranging economic reforms and opened their markets. Both enjoy investment grades from rating agencies, meaning they already compete for capital with leading emerging markets worldwide.

Croatia's economy is expected to grow at 6.5 percent this year, with inflation running at less than four percent. Slovenia, its northern neighbour, will see growth of around four percent this year, experts forecast.

Progress has come at a price. Croatia's tough brand of monetarism has helped to keep inflation under control, but the strong currency, the kuna, hurts exporters and has contributed to widescale unemployment, estimated at 17 percent.

In Slovenia, where per-capita incomes have reached almost western levels, unemployment is also running at alarmingly high levels, expected to approach 14 percent this year. The country is pushing hard to join the EU and by all standards would qualify for early entry, were it not for some of its anti-foreign investment policies.
PROBLEMS MORE SEVERE FURTHER SOUTH
Yet those problems are small compared to the challenges most of their neighbours are facing, analysts say.

Deteriorating quality of life and complete disillusionment with the slow pace of political reforms have contributed to widespread popular unrest in countries such as Albania, Bulgaria or Serbia, which have the region's worst economies.
In Albania, Europe's poorhouse, the failure of a string of pyramid schemes has sparked armed rebellion.

The ensuing anarchy and chaos means some positive economic developments in the last few years may be undone, especially if any future government is forced to compensate for losses incurred by the population in the pyramid schemes.

In Yugoslavia, months of street protests have forced Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to acknowledge opposition victories in local elections and he faces losing power in national polls later this year. But on the economic front, the hardline socialist government is not moving an inch, fearing that any belt tightening would completely ruin its electoral chances.

Public revenues have dropped dramatically, output and wages are plummeting while the trade deficit, unemployment and prices are on the rise, stirring memories of the economic disaster suffered by the country in the early 1990s.
The economy, hurt by four years of war-related sanctions, is reeling under the lack of fresh money from abroad, seen as the only hope for salvaging the country from complete collapse.
As in neighbouring Bulgaria, analysts say a deal with the International Monetary Fund, enabling Yugoslavia's return to the world's financial markets, is the only way forward.
The government acknowledges this necessity, but drags its feet on necessary reforms, such as large-scale privatisation and opening up the economy to foreign investment.
ISOLATIONISM AND NATIONALISM PREVENT REFORM
This kind of isolationism is taking hold not only in Yugoslavia, but across the region, analysts say.

Slovenia, which has just introduced legislation to keep foreign investment at bay, is another example for many of the reform states' refusal to accept the reality of economic interdependence and openness, they say.
"It makes no sense whatsoever from an economic point of view. They really have to think that over," Svoboda said.
But unless the poltical elite in countries such as Yugoslavia make way for more reform-minded leaders, the economic outlook remains grim, he added.
"Just look at those gentlemen in Serbia or Albania. You're dealing with the same kind of people you were dealing with before 1989. It's just a different label."
GLIMMER OF HOPE IN ROMANIA AND BULGARIA
Signs of hope are emerging in both Bulgaria and Romania.

After month-long mass protests, Bulgarian President Peter Stoyanov last month brokered a deal providing for early elections and a caretaker cabinet, which has set out to cut state spending, shut down loss-making state enterprises and crack down on corruption.
Romania's new centrist government has vowed to liberalise prices and bring down inflation and deficits with the help of international financial institutions.
There is light at the end of the tunnel, but it will take a while until most southeastern Europeans will get to see it.
"Maybe in 1999 we'll be able to talk of a new take-off, a new kind of economic optimism. But for now, realism is the order of the day," said Svoboda.
